claim: Whole-cell recordings were targeted to two classes of inhibitory GABAergic neurons in layer 2/3 of the barrel cortex of awake head-restrained mice.
source: Here, we targeted whole-cell recordings to two classes of inhibitory GABAergic neurons in layer 2/3 of the barrel cortex of awake head-restrained mice and correlated spontaneous membrane potential dynamics with cortical state and whisking behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a methodological approach taken in the study.

claim: Spontaneous membrane potential dynamics were correlated with cortical state and whisking behavior.
source: Here, we targeted whole-cell recordings to two classes of inhibitory GABAergic neurons in layer 2/3 of the barrel cortex of awake head-restrained mice and correlated spontaneous membrane potential dynamics with cortical state and whisking behavior.
evidence: This is stated as part of the experimental approach in the abstract.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of single layer 2/3 excitatory neurons was used to measure unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (uEPSPs) across states.
source: Using optogenetic stimulation of single layer 2/3 excitatory neurons we measured unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (uEPSPs) across states.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a methodological approach.

claim: During active states, parvalbumin-expressing neurons depolarized.
source: During active states, characterized by whisking and reduced low-frequency activity in the local field potential, parvalbumin-expressing neurons depolarized and, albeit in a small number of recordings, received uEPSPs with increased amplitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: During active states, parvalbumin-expressing neurons received uEPSPs with increased amplitude, albeit in a small number of recordings.
source: During active states, characterized by whisking and reduced low-frequency activity in the local field potential, parvalbumin-expressing neurons depolarized and, albeit in a small number of recordings, received uEPSPs with increased amplitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract with acknowledgment of limited sample size.

claim: Active states are characterized by whisking and reduced low-frequency activity in the local field potential.
source: During active states, characterized by whisking and reduced low-frequency activity in the local field potential, parvalbumin-expressing neurons depolarized and, albeit in a small number of recordings, received uEPSPs with increased amplitude.
evidence: This is a definition of active states provided in the abstract.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing neurons hyperpolarized during active states.
source: In contrast, somatostatin-expressing neurons hyperpolarized and reduced firing rates during active states without consistent change in uEPSP amplitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing neurons reduced firing rates during active states.
source: In contrast, somatostatin-expressing neurons hyperpolarized and reduced firing rates during active states without consistent change in uEPSP amplitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing neurons showed no consistent change in uEPSP amplitude during active states.
source: In contrast, somatostatin-expressing neurons hyperpolarized and reduced firing rates during active states without consistent change in uEPSP amplitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: Distinct genetically-defined cell classes have different state-dependent patterns of activity.
source: These results further our understanding of neocortical inhibitory neuron function in awake mice and are consistent with the hypothesis that distinct genetically-defined cell classes have different state-dependent patterns of activity.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis consistent with the results in the abstract.

claim: In cortical excitatory neurons, reduced low-frequency neocortical EEG or local field potential (LFP) activity consistently correlates with a decrease in membrane potential (Vm) variance.
source: In cortical excitatory neurons, reduced low-frequency neocortical EEG or local field potential (LFP) activity, such as that observed during active behaviors, consistently correlates with a decrease in membrane potential (Vm) variance through a reduction in the amplitude of low-frequency Vm fluctuations, accompanied, on average, by Vm depolarization (Steriade et al., 2001; Timofeev et al., 2001; Crochet and Petersen, 2006; Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Yamashita et al., 2013; Bennett et al., 2013; Polack et al., 2013; Schneider et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Reduced low-frequency neocortical activity in excitatory neurons is accompanied by a reduction in the amplitude of low-frequency Vm fluctuations.
source: In cortical excitatory neurons, reduced low-frequency neocortical EEG or local field potential (LFP) activity, such as that observed during active behaviors, consistently correlates with a decrease in membrane potential (Vm) variance through a reduction in the amplitude of low-frequency Vm fluctuations, accompanied, on average, by Vm depolarization (Steriade et al., 2001; Timofeev et al., 2001; Crochet and Petersen, 2006; Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Yamashita et al., 2013; Bennett et al., 2013; Polack et al., 2013; Schneider et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Reduced low-frequency neocortical activity in excitatory neurons is accompanied, on average, by Vm depolarization.
source: In cortical excitatory neurons, reduced low-frequency neocortical EEG or local field potential (LFP) activity, such as that observed during active behaviors, consistently correlates with a decrease in membrane potential (Vm) variance through a reduction in the amplitude of low-frequency Vm fluctuations, accompanied, on average, by Vm depolarization (Steriade et al., 2001; Timofeev et al., 2001; Crochet and Petersen, 2006; Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Yamashita et al., 2013; Bennett et al., 2013; Polack et al., 2013; Schneider et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Much less is known regarding Vm and its relationship to action potential (AP) firing in inhibitory GABAergic neurons during various states of awake neocortical activity and during active behaviors.
source: Much less is known regarding Vm and its relationship to action potential (AP) firing in inhibitory GABAergic neurons during various states of awake neocortical activity and during active behaviors.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Fast-spiking inhibitory neurons in layer 2/3 mouse primary somatosensory whisker barrel cortex (wS1) decrease AP firing during whisking with little change in mean Vm but decreased Vm variance.
source: In layer 2/3 (L2/3) mouse primary somatosensory whisker barrel cortex (wS1), fast-spiking inhibitory neurons were found to decrease AP firing during whisking with little change in mean Vm but decreased Vm variance (Gentet et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons in L2/3 mouse visual cortex exhibited Vm depolarization accompanied by an increase in AP firing during locomotion.
source: In comparison, parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons in L2/3 mouse visual cortex exhibited Vm depolarization accompanied by an increase in AP firing during locomotion (Polack et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing (Sst) neurons are inhibited during whisking in L2/3 of wS1.
source: Disparities also exist amongst somatostatin-expressing (Sst) neurons, which are inhibited during whisking in L2/3 of wS1 (Gentet et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013; Muñoz et al., 2017), and either excited or inhibited by locomotion in L2/3 visual cortex (Polack et al., 2013; Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing (Sst) neurons are either excited or inhibited by locomotion in L2/3 visual cortex.
source: Disparities also exist amongst somatostatin-expressing (Sst) neurons, which are inhibited during whisking in L2/3 of wS1 (Gentet et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013; Muñoz et al., 2017), and either excited or inhibited by locomotion in L2/3 visual cortex (Polack et al., 2013; Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Changes in synaptic efficacy could contribute to driving state-dependent Vm dynamics.
source: Mechanistically, changes in synaptic efficacy could contribute to driving state-dependent Vm dynamics, but in vivo measurements of synaptic transmission have largely been carried out under anesthesia (Matsumura et al., 1996; Crochet et al., 2005; Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Jouhanneau et al., 2015; Pala and Petersen, 2015; Safari et al., 2017; Jouhanneau et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis stated in the introduction.

claim: In vivo measurements of synaptic transmission have largely been carried out under anesthesia.
source: Mechanistically, changes in synaptic efficacy could contribute to driving state-dependent Vm dynamics, but in vivo measurements of synaptic transmission have largely been carried out under anesthesia (Matsumura et al., 1996; Crochet et al., 2005; Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Jouhanneau et al., 2015; Pala and Petersen, 2015; Safari et al., 2017; Jouhanneau et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Two-photon targeted whole-cell recordings were made of PV neurons expressing tdTomato in L2/3 of the C2 barrel column of wS1 in awake, head-restrained mice.
source: We made two-photon targeted whole-cell recordings of PV (Figure 1A) (Hippenmeyer et al., 2005) and Sst (Figure 1B) (Taniguchi et al., 2011) neurons expressing tdTomato (Madisen et al., 2010) in L2/3 of the C2 barrel column of wS1 in awake, head-restrained mice.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: Two-photon targeted whole-cell recordings were made of Sst neurons expressing tdTomato in L2/3 of the C2 barrel column of wS1 in awake, head-restrained mice.
source: We made two-photon targeted whole-cell recordings of PV (Figure 1A) (Hippenmeyer et al., 2005) and Sst (Figure 1B) (Taniguchi et al., 2011) neurons expressing tdTomato (Madisen et al., 2010) in L2/3 of the C2 barrel column of wS1 in awake, head-restrained mice.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: Nearby LFP was recorded simultaneously with whole-cell recordings.
source: Simultaneously, we recorded nearby LFP and conducted high speed filming of whisker movements to define cortical states and whisking-related behavioral states.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: High speed filming of whisker movements was conducted to define cortical states and whisking-related behavioral states.
source: Simultaneously, we recorded nearby LFP and conducted high speed filming of whisker movements to define cortical states and whisking-related behavioral states.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: Periods of high and low LFP power in the 1–5 Hz frequency band were identified.
source: We identified periods of high and low LFP power in the 1–5 Hz frequency band, as the amplitude of low frequency activity is known to correlate with various levels of arousal and to be modulated by movement (Steriade, 2000; Gervasoni et al., 2004; Crochet and Petersen, 2006; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: The amplitude of low frequency activity is known to correlate with various levels of arousal and to be modulated by movement.
source: We identified periods of high and low LFP power in the 1–5 Hz frequency band, as the amplitude of low frequency activity is known to correlate with various levels of arousal and to be modulated by movement (Steriade, 2000; Gervasoni et al., 2004; Crochet and Petersen, 2006; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Epochs with and without whisking were determined based on the velocity of the C2 whisker.
source: Epochs with and without whisking were determined based on the velocity of the C2 whisker (Figure 1A,B) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: Cortical states with high 1–5 Hz LFP power largely occurred during non-whisking periods.
source: Cortical states with high 1–5 Hz LFP power largely occurred during non-whisking periods, whereas whisking periods were dominated by low 1–5 Hz LFP power (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Whisking periods were dominated by low 1–5 Hz LFP power.
source: Cortical states with high 1–5 Hz LFP power largely occurred during non-whisking periods, whereas whisking periods were dominated by low 1–5 Hz LFP power (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Quiet periods are defined as epochs with high 1–5 Hz LFP power without whisker movement.
source: In further analyses, we therefore distinguished the two predominant non-overlapping states: Quiet periods defined as epochs with high 1–5 Hz LFP power without whisker movement, and Active periods defined as epochs with low 1–5 Hz LFP power accompanied by whisker movement.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the results section.

claim: Active periods are defined as epochs with low 1–5 Hz LFP power accompanied by whisker movement.
source: In further analyses, we therefore distinguished the two predominant non-overlapping states: Quiet periods defined as epochs with high 1–5 Hz LFP power without whisker movement, and Active periods defined as epochs with low 1–5 Hz LFP power accompanied by whisker movement.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the results section.

claim: During Active states, PV neurons reduced Vm standard deviation.
source: During Active states, PV neurons depolarized (Figure 2A), reduced Vm standard deviation (Figure 2B), and reduced AP firing rate (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: During Active states, PV neurons reduced AP firing rate.
source: During Active states, PV neurons depolarized (Figure 2A), reduced Vm standard deviation (Figure 2B), and reduced AP firing rate (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: During Active states, PV neurons reduced the amplitude of slow-frequency Vm fluctuations.
source: During Active states, PV neurons also reduced the amplitude of slow-frequency Vm fluctuations (Figure 2D,E), and decreased Vm vs LFP cross-correlation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: During Active states, PV neurons decreased Vm vs LFP cross-correlation.
source: During Active states, PV neurons also reduced the amplitude of slow-frequency Vm fluctuations (Figure 2D,E), and decreased Vm vs LFP cross-correlation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Vm of Sst neurons did not change in standard deviation during Active states.
source: In contrast, Vm of Sst neurons hyperpolarized during Active states (Figure 2A) without a change in Vm standard deviation (Figure 2B), giving rise to a reduced AP firing rate (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sst neurons had low amplitude slow-frequency Vm fluctuations during both Quiet and Active states.
source: Sst neurons had low amplitude slow-frequency Vm fluctuations during both Quiet and Active states (Figure 2D,E), and Vm of Sst neurons showed little correlation with LFP, irrespective of state (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Vm of Sst neurons showed little correlation with LFP, irrespective of state.
source: Sst neurons had low amplitude slow-frequency Vm fluctuations during both Quiet and Active states (Figure 2D,E), and Vm of Sst neurons showed little correlation with LFP, irrespective of state (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The Vm differences between PV and Sst neurons were not due to overall differences in cortical states or whisking-related behavior across different genotypes of mice.
source: The Vm differences between PV and Sst neurons were not due to overall differences in cortical states or whisking-related behavior across different genotypes of mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PV neurons may be relatively more strongly modulated by cortical state.
source: Separate analyses of whisking-related and cortical state-related Vm modulation suggested that PV neurons may be relatively more strongly modulated by cortical state, whereas Sst neurons may be relatively more strongly modulated by whisking (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Sst neurons may be relatively more strongly modulated by whisking.
source: Separate analyses of whisking-related and cortical state-related Vm modulation suggested that PV neurons may be relatively more strongly modulated by cortical state, whereas Sst neurons may be relatively more strongly modulated by whisking (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Enhanced efficacy of local excitatory synaptic input onto PV neurons could contribute to the overall depolarization of PV neurons in Active states.
source: Enhanced efficacy of local excitatory synaptic input onto PV neurons could contribute to the overall depolarization of PV neurons in Active states, and equally decreased efficacy of excitatory synaptic input onto Sst neurons could contribute to the overall hyperpolarisation of Sst neurons in Active states.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results section.

claim: Decreased efficacy of excitatory synaptic input onto Sst neurons could contribute to the overall hyperpolarisation of Sst neurons in Active states.
source: Enhanced efficacy of local excitatory synaptic input onto PV neurons could contribute to the overall depolarization of PV neurons in Active states, and equally decreased efficacy of excitatory synaptic input onto Sst neurons could contribute to the overall hyperpolarisation of Sst neurons in Active states.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results section.

claim: Chronos was expressed in a single L2/3 excitatory neuron per mouse through two-photon targeted single-cell electroporation.
source: Through two-photon targeted single-cell electroporation (Kitamura et al., 2008; Pala and Petersen, 2015), we expressed a fast channelrhodopsin, Chronos (Klapoetke et al., 2014), in a single L2/3 excitatory neuron per mouse (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: Brief pulses of light (1 ms, 1 Hz) delivered using a 470 nm LED elicited highly reliable, time-locked single APs at short latency in Chronos-expressing neurons across both Quiet and Active states.
source: Brief pulses of light (1 ms, 1 Hz) delivered using a 470 nm LED elicited highly reliable, time-locked single APs at short latency in Chronos-expressing neurons across both Quiet and Active states (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), evoking unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (uEPSPs) in PV (Figure 3D–F) and Sst neurons (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Light stimulation evoked unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (uEPSPs) in PV neurons.
source: Brief pulses of light (1 ms, 1 Hz) delivered using a 470 nm LED elicited highly reliable, time-locked single APs at short latency in Chronos-expressing neurons across both Quiet and Active states (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), evoking unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (uEPSPs) in PV (Figure 3D–F) and Sst neurons (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: Light stimulation evoked unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (uEPSPs) in Sst neurons.
source: Brief pulses of light (1 ms, 1 Hz) delivered using a 470 nm LED elicited highly reliable, time-locked single APs at short latency in Chronos-expressing neurons across both Quiet and Active states (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), evoking unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (uEPSPs) in PV (Figure 3D–F) and Sst neurons (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3G–I.

claim: The uEPSPs were faster in PV neurons than in Sst neurons.
source: The uEPSPs were faster in PV neurons than in Sst neurons, but with overall similar amplitudes (Figure 4A,C Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: uEPSPs in PV and Sst neurons had overall similar amplitudes.
source: The uEPSPs were faster in PV neurons than in Sst neurons, but with overall similar amplitudes (Figure 4A,C Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was an increase in uEPSP amplitude in PV neurons (n = 5 cells, p=0.031, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test) during Active states compared to Quiet states.
source: In the small number of synaptically-connected postsynaptic neurons, we found an increase in uEPSP amplitude in PV neurons (n = 5 cells, p=0.031, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test) during Active states compared to Quiet states, but no consistent change in uEPSP amplitude in Sst neurons (n = 5 cells, p=0.22, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: There was no consistent change in uEPSP amplitude in Sst neurons (n = 5 cells, p=0.22, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test) during Active states compared to Quiet states.
source: In the small number of synaptically-connected postsynaptic neurons, we found an increase in uEPSP amplitude in PV neurons (n = 5 cells, p=0.031, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test) during Active states compared to Quiet states, but no consistent change in uEPSP amplitude in Sst neurons (n = 5 cells, p=0.22, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: In the Active state, the baseline Vm (from which uEPSPs were evoked) was more depolarized for PV neurons.
source: In the Active state, the baseline Vm (from which uEPSPs were evoked) was more depolarized for PV neurons, but more hyperpolarized for Sst neurons (Figure 4F), in agreement with the overall state-dependent Vm changes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In the Active state, the baseline Vm (from which uEPSPs were evoked) was more hyperpolarized for Sst neurons.
source: In the Active state, the baseline Vm (from which uEPSPs were evoked) was more depolarized for PV neurons, but more hyperpolarized for Sst neurons (Figure 4F), in agreement with the overall state-dependent Vm changes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The results suggest an enhancement of local excitatory synaptic transmission onto PV neurons during Active states.
source: Altogether, these results suggest an enhancement of local excitatory synaptic transmission onto PV neurons during Active states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the uEPSP amplitude data.

claim: The hyperpolarization of Sst neurons is thought to be driven by increased firing of VIP-expressing GABAergic neurons, which strongly inhibit Sst neurons.
source: The hyperpolarization of Sst neurons is thought to be driven by increased firing of VIP-expressing GABAergic neurons, which strongly inhibit Sst neurons (Lee et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The reduction in AP firing rate of Sst neurons during Active states may disinhibit distal dendrites of nearby excitatory neurons.
source: The reduction in AP firing rate of Sst neurons during Active states may disinhibit distal dendrites of nearby excitatory neurons (Gentet et al., 2012), perhaps promoting non-linear dendritic excitation important for sensorimotor integration and perceptual decision-making (Xu et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sst neurons in L2/3 mouse barrel cortex are functionally relatively uncoupled from the surrounding neuronal network.
source: Sst neurons in L2/3 mouse barrel cortex are therefore functionally relatively uncoupled from the surrounding neuronal network, within which all other cell-types show highly correlated low frequency Vm fluctuations (Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Gentet et al., 2010; Gentet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the low correlation with LFP and citations to prior work.

claim: All other cell-types in L2/3 mouse barrel cortex show highly correlated low frequency Vm fluctuations.
source: Sst neurons in L2/3 mouse barrel cortex are therefore functionally relatively uncoupled from the surrounding neuronal network, within which all other cell-types show highly correlated low frequency Vm fluctuations (Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Gentet et al., 2010; Gentet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sst neurons receive excitatory synaptic input, which shows strong frequency-dependent facilitation.
source: In addition to prominent inhibitory input from VIP neurons, Sst neurons receive excitatory synaptic input, which shows strong frequency-dependent facilitation (Reyes et al., 1998; Kapfer et al., 2007; Silberberg and Markram, 2007; Pala and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Short-term synaptic plasticity together with cell-type- and layer-specific circuits likely contribute to the relatively decoupled Vm dynamics of Sst neurons compared to other types of nearby neurons.
source: Short-term synaptic plasticity together with cell-type- and layer-specific circuits likely contribute to the relatively decoupled Vm dynamics of Sst neurons compared to other types of nearby neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior knowledge and current findings.

claim: Nicotinic enhancement of uEPSPs has recently been reported on Sst neurons in wS1 of anesthetised mice.
source: Nicotinic enhancement of uEPSPs has recently been reported on Sst neurons in wS1 of anesthetised mice (Urban-Ciecko et al., 2018), and acetylcholine is known to be released during whisking (Eggermann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Acetylcholine is known to be released during whisking.
source: Nicotinic enhancement of uEPSPs has recently been reported on Sst neurons in wS1 of anesthetised mice (Urban-Ciecko et al., 2018), and acetylcholine is known to be released during whisking (Eggermann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: During Quiet states PV neurons were on average hyperpolarized.
source: During Quiet states PV neurons were on average hyperpolarized (Figure 2A) and exhibited large Vm variance (Figure 2B) in the slow frequency range (Figure 2D,E) highly correlated with the LFP (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: During Quiet states PV neurons exhibited large Vm variance.
source: During Quiet states PV neurons were on average hyperpolarized (Figure 2A) and exhibited large Vm variance (Figure 2B) in the slow frequency range (Figure 2D,E) highly correlated with the LFP (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: During Quiet states PV neurons exhibited large Vm variance in the slow frequency range highly correlated with the LFP.
source: During Quiet states PV neurons were on average hyperpolarized (Figure 2A) and exhibited large Vm variance (Figure 2B) in the slow frequency range (Figure 2D,E) highly correlated with the LFP (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, 2E, and 2F.

claim: During Active states, the Vm of PV neurons depolarized together with a reduction in Vm variance, Vm slow fluctuations and Vm correlation with LFP.
source: Conversely, during Active states, the Vm of PV neurons depolarized together with a reduction in Vm variance, Vm slow fluctuations and Vm correlation with LFP.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Despite depolarization, the AP firing rate of PV neurons reduced significantly during the Active state.
source: Despite depolarization, the AP firing rate of PV neurons reduced significantly during the Active state (Figure 2C), presumably because the decreased Vm variance prevented an increased frequency of Vm excursions above AP threshold.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The decreased Vm variance in PV neurons during Active states presumably prevented an increased frequency of Vm excursions above AP threshold.
source: Despite depolarization, the AP firing rate of PV neurons reduced significantly during the Active state (Figure 2C), presumably because the decreased Vm variance prevented an increased frequency of Vm excursions above AP threshold.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the observed data.

claim: Decreased firing of fast-spiking neurons was previously noted in L2/3 of wS1 during whisking.
source: Consistent with these observations, decreased firing of fast-spiking neurons was also previously noted in L2/3 of wS1 during whisking (Gentet et al., 2010), and during licking events accompanied by whisking in a whisker detection task (Sachidhanandam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Decreased firing of fast-spiking neurons was previously noted during licking events accompanied by whisking in a whisker detection task.
source: Consistent with these observations, decreased firing of fast-spiking neurons was also previously noted in L2/3 of wS1 during whisking (Gentet et al., 2010), and during licking events accompanied by whisking in a whisker detection task (Sachidhanandam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A reduction in the firing rate of PV neurons in L2/3 of wS1 typically accompanies whisking.
source: These results appear to suggest that a reduction in the firing rate of PV neurons in L2/3 of wS1 typically accompanies whisking.
evidence: This is an inference based on current and prior findings.

claim: The reduced firing rates of PV neurons during Active states will presumably disinhibit the surrounding neuronal network.
source: The reduced firing rates of PV neurons during Active states will presumably disinhibit the surrounding neuronal network, perhaps promoting synaptic computations amongst the excitatory pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed data.

claim: An increased amplitude of incoming L2/3 excitatory synaptic input could contribute to driving the depolarized average Vm in PV neurons during the Active cortical state.
source: An increased amplitude of incoming L2/3 excitatory synaptic input could contribute to driving the depolarized average Vm in PV neurons during the Active cortical state (Figures 2A and 4F).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed data in Figures 2A and 4F.

claim: Depolarization reduces the electrical driving force for glutamatergic conductances and therefore cannot explain increased amplitude of uEPSPs.
source: Depolarization reduces the electrical driving force for glutamatergic conductances and therefore cannot explain increased amplitude of uEPSPs.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: Six 5–10 week old female and male PV-IRES-Cre mice were used in accordance with protocols approved by the Swiss Federal Veterinary Office (authorisation VD1628).
source: Six 5–10 week old female and male PV-IRES-Cre (Hippenmeyer et al., 2005) mice and five 5–10 week old female and male Sst-IRES-Cre (Taniguchi et al., 2011) mice crossed with CAG-Lox-STOP-Lox-tdTomato (LSL-tdTomato) mice (Madisen et al., 2010) were used in accordance with protocols approved by the Swiss Federal Veterinary Office (authorisation VD1628).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the animals used.

claim: Five 5–10 week old female and male Sst-IRES-Cre mice were used in accordance with protocols approved by the Swiss Federal Veterinary Office (authorisation VD1628).
source: Six 5–10 week old female and male PV-IRES-Cre (Hippenmeyer et al., 2005) mice and five 5–10 week old female and male Sst-IRES-Cre (Taniguchi et al., 2011) mice crossed with CAG-Lox-STOP-Lox-tdTomato (LSL-tdTomato) mice (Madisen et al., 2010) were used in accordance with protocols approved by the Swiss Federal Veterinary Office (authorisation VD1628).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the animals used.

claim: Mice were maintained under 1–2% isoflurane anesthesia while being implanted with a custom-made head-holder and a recording chamber.
source: Mice were maintained under 1–2% isoflurane anesthesia while being implanted with a custom-made head-holder and a recording chamber.
